pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 5-6 (Y1). Recall number bonds — addition AND related subtraction facts — within 20: know pairs of single-digit numbers summing up to 20 and derive the subtractions (8+5=13, 13−5=8). Extends bonds-to-10 to the full within-20 set; the fact base for KS1 mental calculation.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): 'represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts within 20'; non-statutory: memorise and reason with bonds to 10 and 20 in several forms (9+7=16; 16−7=9; 7=16−9).
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.6 add/subtract within 20; 1.OA.8 work with the unknown in various positions.
• Operational details — Present bonds as FACT FAMILIES from the start: each bond generates two additions and two subtractions and can be written with the unknown anywhere (7=16−9). Build recall from bonds to 10 plus bridging (making-ten) and doubles, then firm up with retrieval practice. The deliberate inclusion of related subtraction is the point — subtraction facts should come from known additions, not be learned separately.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 5): recall bonds to 10 and derive some within-20 sums via making ten. Tier B (age 5-6): recall within-20 bonds and give the related subtraction fact. Tier C (age 6): flexibly state any member of a within-20 fact family, including missing-number forms (7 = 16 − ?).
bestPractices: Teach every bond as a fact family (a+b, b+a, whole−a, whole−b) so one known fact yields four, and subtraction is derived from addition.
Present the facts in several forms including unknown-in-different-positions (7 = 16 − 9) to build flexibility and pre-empt the 'answer after =' habit.
Build within-20 recall from bonds to 10 + making-ten + doubles rather than as fresh rote facts.
Use fact-family triangles and part-whole models so the relationship among the three numbers is explicit.
Consolidate with short, frequent, interleaved retrieval; keep a reconstructing strategy available for slips.
keyRepresentations: Fact-family triangle (whole and two parts) generating four facts
Ten-frames (one full, one partial) for bridging bonds
Equation sets showing a bond in all four forms and missing-number variants
commonMisconceptions: Learning additions and subtractions as separate lists rather than as fact families, doubling the memory load and leaving subtraction weak.
Recalling only the canonical form (8+5) and struggling with 5+8 or 13−8.
Rejecting missing-number/reordered forms (7 = 16 − 9) because = is read as 'answer here'.
Counting rather than recalling, especially for bridging facts.
Confusing bonds of different totals when facts aren't tied to a clear whole.

learn.summary: Ages 5-6 (Y1): recall number bonds within 20 as fact families, so each addition fact (8+5=13) hands over its related subtractions (13−5=8, 13−8=5) rather than being memorised separately. Facts should appear in all four forms and with the unknown in any position (7=16−9) to pre-empt the 'answer-after-equals' habit. Within-20 recall is built from bonds-to-10 plus making-ten (bridging) and doubles, then firmed with short, frequent interleaved retrieval, while a reconstructing strategy stays available for slips.

activities.title: Fact-family machine: one relationship, four facts
feedback: If a child recalls 8+5 fluently but re-counts 13−5 from scratch, prompt 'think of the addition — 8 and 5 make 13, so 13 take away 5 leaves...' and point to the same triangle.
If a child rejects 7 = 16 − 9 because '= means the answer comes next', re-read it as 'what goes with 9 to make 16?' and show both the 9+7=16 and the 7=16−9 forms around the same whole.
If a child counts on by ones for a crossing-ten sum, model making ten (8+2+3 for 8+5) using one full and one partial ten-frame, then return to recall.
If a child confuses bonds of different totals, re-anchor each fact to its clearly labelled whole in the part-whole model before practising.
activities.rationale: A manipulable part-whole/triangle model makes the four-facts structure explicit and lets the child regenerate the whole family, which supports relational understanding of the equals sign and deriving subtraction from addition. Live rewriting and 'cover a corner' missing-number practice are concrete ways to show the structure and target the equals-sign misconception; they are optional illustrative mechanisms, not the only route.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts within 20, in several forms including unknown in different positions (9+7=16; 16−7=9; 7=16−9).
Teaching bonds as fact families (deriving subtraction from addition) and in varied forms builds flexible recall and relational understanding of =.
learnerActions: Set a whole of 13 with two parts, 8 and 5, in a part-whole triangle (whole at the top, parts in the lower corners).
Read the four facts that the relationship generates: 8+5=13, 5+8=13, 13−8=5, 13−5=8. Say each one aloud.

Change a part (e.g. make the parts 7 and 6 with whole 13) and watch all four equations rewrite, so you see the same structure holds for every bond (for a double such as 6+6=12, the four forms reduce to two different facts: 6+6=12 and 12−6=6).

Use a 'cover a corner' mode: hide one number and say the missing one. Then set a new, clearly labelled whole (e.g. whole 16 with parts 7 and 9) and practise missing-number forms such as 7 = 16 − ? and 16 − ? = 9.
Practise shaky family members again in short interleaved rounds until the four facts come quickly from recall or near-instant derivation.
activities.intendedInsight: One relationship among three numbers IS four facts: learning 8+5 gives you 13−5 and 13−8 for free, so subtraction is derived from addition rather than memorised as a separate list.

activities.title: Build within-20 recall from bonds-to-10, making-ten and doubles
feedback: If a child finger-counts 9,10,11,12,13 for 8+5, the sum is not yet recalled — practise making-ten explicitly and re-check bonds to 10 underneath.

If small facts are instant but teen facts are shaky, focus practice on the shaky teen facts (often the crossing-ten ones), while keeping secure small bonds in occasional mixed review rather than re-drilling them.
Praise a correct reconstruction (making-ten) as a valid strategy to keep available for slips, while moving toward quick recall.
activities.rationale: Grounding within-20 recall in bonds-to-10 plus bridging and doubles reduces memory load and gives a fallback strategy, matching the stated progression toward the fact base of KS1 mental calculation. The making-ten and doubles strategies come from the pedagogy best-practices rather than from a directly supporting source claim.
learnerActions: Re-secure bonds to 10 first (e.g. 6+4, 7+3) so they are instant.
For a crossing-ten sum like 8+5, split the second number to make ten: 8+2=10, then 10+3=13. Use one full ten-frame and one partial frame to show the move.
Use a known double to help a near-double: 6+7 is 6+6+1 or 7+7−1.
State which facts you just KNEW and which you had to work out, then practise the worked-out ones more.
Repeat in short, frequent, mixed sessions rather than one long drill.
activities.intendedInsight: Teen bonds are not fresh rote facts: they can be derived from secure bonds to 10 using making-ten and doubles, and derivation becomes faster recall with spaced practice.

activities.title: Mixed-form retrieval practice across the fact family
feedback: Correct answers to 8+5 and 13−5 are 13 and 8; if a learner offers anything else, re-check with the part-whole whole of 13.

A quick, non-counting response to 13−5 immediately after 8+5 shows the fact family is being used; slow re-counting of the subtraction signals it is still being computed from scratch — prompt 'think of the addition'.
Placing missing-number items (7 = 16 − ?) early catches the equals-sign misconception; if missed, re-read as a part-whole question.
activities.rationale: Short targeted retrieval across all forms consolidates recall and assesses whether subtraction is derived from addition. A fixed set of practice items directly targets the facts but is less adaptive than a tool that re-serves shaky items; recognition and completion of items can check facts but does not by itself supply the many spaced repetitions recall requires, so use it for consolidation and quick checking alongside spaced practice.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.6 add/subtract within 20; 1.OA.8 determine the unknown in an equation with the unknown in various positions.
Teaching bonds as fact families (deriving subtraction from addition) and in varied forms builds flexible recall and relational understanding of =.
learnerActions: Answer quick-fire items drawn from all four forms of a family: 8+5=?, 5+8=?, 13−5=?, 13−8=?.
Answer missing-number items with the unknown in different positions: 7 = 16 − ?, 8 + ? = 13, ? − 5 = 8.
Mix additions and their related subtractions back-to-back (8+5 then 13−5) to practise pulling the subtraction from the addition.
Note any item that needed counting and return to it after a making-ten reminder.
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and completing a bond in any form — including the unknown in any position — is the mark of flexible, secure fact-family knowledge.

constraints: Teach each bond as a fact family (a+b, b+a, whole−a, whole−b) from the start so subtraction is derived from addition, not learned as a separate list.
Present facts in several forms, including the unknown in different positions (7 = 16 − 9), to pre-empt reading = as 'answer here'.
A static fact-family/part-whole reference shows the four-facts structure but does not generate retrieval; pair it with active recall practice.

Recognition-only or fixed-item practice can check facts and support relational understanding but does not by itself build the many spaced repetitions recall requires; interleave and space the practice.
Keep a reconstructing strategy (making-ten, doubles) available as a fallback for slips even as quick recall becomes the goal.
Tie every fact to a clearly labelled whole so bonds of different totals are not confused.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Legacy source marked the UK National Curriculum claim as verified; the Common Core (1.OA.6/1.OA.8) and NCETM fact-family claims were marked unverified. Treat the latter two as unverified.

Activity 2's making-ten/doubles derivation progression is drawn from the pedagogy best-practices, not from a source claim that directly supports it, so its sourceClaims list is empty rather than citing topic-only overlaps.

The legacy row asserted bond facts are 'not spatial' and dismissed a 3D treatment; this comparative/necessity claim is not established by the cited sources and has been dropped rather than propagated. Physical models (bead string, rekenrek, ten-frames) are nonetheless useful concrete supports.

Independent re-audit confirmed the source examples are arithmetically correct (8+5=13, 13−5=8, 13−8=5, making-ten 8+2+3, 6+7 as near-double, 7=16−9, 16−?=9→7, 8+?=13→5, ?−5=8→13) and that source-claim attributions exactly copy the cited claims and support the stated principle rather than the topic alone; no critical learner-facing errors were found.

probeDeeper: You knew 8 + 5 = 13 — how does that help with 13 − 5?
What's a quick way to work out 6 + 7 if you don't just know it?
Which of these did you just KNOW, and which did you have to work out?
assess.correctAnswer: 13, 8, 13, 8 — answered rapidly from recall or near-instant derivation (e.g. make-ten), with each subtraction pulled from its related addition fact.

errorPatterns.pattern: No bridging strategy — counts on by ones for teen sums (8+5 counted 9,10,11,12,13 on fingers), so it is not a recalled bond.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Teach make-ten (8+2+3) so crossing-ten sums become derived facts; re-secure bonds to 10 as the foundation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Visible finger-counting, slow, especially on facts that cross ten.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats subtraction as unrelated to addition — re-counts 13−5 from scratch rather than using 8+5=13.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make fact families explicit with part-whole (8+5=13 ↔ 13−5=8, 13−8=5); prompt 'think of the addition'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Fluent on the additions but slow / counting on the subtractions.

errorPatterns.pattern: Small bonds secure but teen / crossing-ten facts shaky — fast under 10, hesitant over 10.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Targeted practice on the crossing-ten facts alone; do not re-drill the already-secure small facts.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Instant recall below ten, hesitation on the bridging facts only.

responseLevels.gap: Counts on by ones for most facts; subtraction re-computed from scratch.
responseLevels.full: Recalls bonds within 20 rapidly and derives the related subtraction facts from them without counting.
responseLevels.partial: Recalls or quickly derives sums but subtraction lags, or crossing-ten facts still counted.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Quick-fire, try not to count on your fingers: what is 8 + 5? … Now 13 − 5? … 6 + 7? … 14 − 6?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch the method and the timing. Fluent recall of bonds within 20 is quick and does not rely on counting on by ones. Placing 13−5 immediately after 8+5 reveals whether the child uses the addition fact (fact family) or re-computes the subtraction from scratch — the signature of true bond knowledge.
